title: I let Claude Fable 5.1 trade 100 USDC for 15 days and kept the trade journal
author: AgentAiLeader
selftext:
Last month I gave Claude Fable 5.1 100 USDC to trade. It could choose positions, pay for market data and execute trades within rules I gave it. I wanted to see what it would actually do with a small live account.

The last recorded portfolio value was $102.79. Data cost 5.08 USDC and gas was about $0.63, so the increase didn't cover those costs, but these costs are basically fixed so would stay the same with a bigger portfolio. Full transparency, the graph shows the saved portfolio values before those costs.

I ran it from September 17 to October 2 using Claude Code scheduled routines, my Claude subscription and Finance District's Agent Wallet. The wallet handled balances, swaps and data payments; GitHub kept the positions, rules and journal between runs. I adjusted the setup as I went.

This version traded crypto on BNB Chain because that's where I configured it. It couldn't just decide to buy an ordinary stock or move to another chain. It paid for data separately on Base through x402. Nansen showed where Smart Money was flowing and how many tracked wallets were involved, while CoinGecko surfaced trending pools with trading volume and liquidity data.

The rules allowed up to 45% across BTC, ETH and BNB, up to three smaller 10 USDC positions, and a cash buffer. Smaller entries needed liquidity and security checks, plus hourly chart conditions. One pattern required price above EMA20, with EMA20 above EMA50, alongside RSI and volume checks. It had to record what would invalidate the trade before buying.

Initially it checked every four hours, but after an alt token dropped significantly between checks, I added Sonnet watchers, eventually targeting every 15 minutes. Fable looked for opportunities; Sonnet watched existing positions and attempted exits. A stop threshold still didn't guarantee the price it would get.

One bug I discovered on the go, on September 25 it sold half a RHEA position, then the rest 15 minutes later because the same condition was still true. I changed the instructions to remember the price peak at the partial sale and require a new higher peak before another trailing exit. The entry price stop still applied. NEAR was a losing example: about 5.4% lost on the portion sold after its moving average condition failed.

The data spending needed work too. Nansen cost 0.05 USDC per request for Smart Money flows and tracked wallet counts; CoinGecko cost 0.01 for trending pools, activity and liquidity. There were 85 Nansen payments and 83 CoinGecko payments. The watchers used free price data.

I found a run that bought both feeds with all three smaller position slots already full, then made no trade. Later instructions checked for room and cash before buying discovery data. I still really don't know whether the paid feeds improved returns.

I also temporarily slowed the main trader to six hour checks and reduced the candidates it examined when my weekly Fable 5.1 credits ran low. That subscription helped me with other wokr stuff too, so I can't give an experiment only Claude cost.

The reviews looked at rejected tokens afterwards, including rallies it missed, and checked prices after exits. One review found 5 of 15 liquidity rejections had missed a more liquid pool for the same token. I added another pool lookup. Neither weekly review changed a strategy parameter, so I wouldn't claim it learned to trade better.

There are some gaps in the result. Positions were still open at the final snapshot, and the recorded portfolio excluded the gas reserve, including about $1.49 moved into it, plus small leftover token balances.

Tbh 15 days is a very short test. A few good market days could make a big difference, and I didn't compare it with buy and hold. But to be fare on the agent, it did sell its BNB, BTCB and ETH core positions into USDC when their trend exit rules triggered and they ended up going down another 2% so it was a good choice, all while keeping a smaller CAP position open. I'd like to see how it behaves through a longer bear market. This run doesn't answer that, especially since I changed rules along the way.

Next time I'd keep the rules fixed, track all costs and compare against buy and hold and the same strategy using free data. I'd also test whether ordinary code can handle the routine price checks, with Claude investigating exceptions.

I'm curious about testing tokenized stocks on Robinhood Chain or  BNB Chain. This run only traded crypto.

The wallet is public:[ BNB Chain trades](https://bscscan.com/address/0x6946cF18b64f7C1cc3456f0eDE93e1cf767927Eb) and[ Base data payments](https://basescan.org/address/0x6946cF18b64f7C1cc3456f0eDE93e1cf767927Eb). I shared an earlier write up in r/x402 last week, more focused on payments.

Mostly wanted to share my experience and see if anyone is trying something similar. What would you improve/change? Which decisions have you found worth giving to a model, and which would you leave to fixed rules?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
The next run could test the paid feeds without risking two live portfolios. At each Fable decision, save the prompt state before adding Nansen, generate a free-data-only decision, then add the 0.05 USDC Smart Money response and generate the paid-data decision. Execute only the assigned arm, but log both recommendations and whether Nansen changed the token, size, or trade/no-trade outcome. Do the same for CoinGecko’s 0.01 USDC pool data.

That would show whether the 85 Nansen and 83 CoinGecko calls affected decisions at all, before asking whether they improved returns. I’d also keep Sonnet’s 15-minute exit rules fixed for both arms. The chart’s $102.79 is gross of the stated data and gas costs, so decision influence is the cleaner first test than P&L over 15 days.

replies.author: AgentAiLeader
replies.body: Thank you, I like this idea. And I think I might actually implement this on a dry run. Basically have Claude log the decisions, trade ledger and portfolio value with free data vs paid and compare the results. The only funds moving would be the x402 data payments to Nansen and Coingecko which shouldn't be too high at $0.06 per run.

replies.body: You do have a point there. I did bounce the initial rules and some of the on the go changes with Claude, so I would say even that part was a bit of a mix too. But you're right, in the end I was teh one approving the final changes that were implemented

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Thanks for sharing the full journal, including the bugs and the costs. To answer your last question, I'd leave the stops, sizing and exits to fixed rules, since you already saw a rule repeat itself on the RHEA sale. I'd use the model for the part code can't do, like reading why a token is moving. For the 15 days, a buy-and-hold baseline on the same coins and a free-data version of the same rules would show whether the paid feeds added anything. Cymetica lets you connect your own AI agent and run it in paper mode first, which is a cheaper way to try ideas like this.

replies.author: AgentAiLeader
replies.body:
Thanks, I'll check out Cymetica. Think it will be useful for the paid vs free data dry run I want to do. 

And yeah, I haven't built in any news or event scraping onto this setup. Understanding why a token is moving would definitely be a good addition and interesting element to add to Fable's reasoning and memory.

comments.author: eduard_trades
comments.body:
Similar setup here, but on crypto prop accounts, where one bad exit can end the account. Where I landed:

Fixed code does everything that has to be exact: position size, stops, the firm's daily loss floor, and the order itself. The model never places an order directly. Every signal goes through a risk check that can say no.

Your RHEA double sale is a good example of why. The condition was true twice because nothing remembered the first sale. Code with stored state doesn't forget that. A model re-reading the situation every 15 minutes can.

What I'd leave to a model: reading news and unusual market conditions, explaining why a trade was taken, and flagging what looks off. Judgment, not timing.

On your next run: keeping the rules fixed matters more than anything else on your list. Every change mid-test resets what you can learn from it. I learned that the expensive way, my own backtest had a bug in moved stops that made a losing strategy look profitable.

replies.author: AgentAiLeader
replies.body:
It was a few prompts rather than one. A main trader Fable 5.1 every 4 hours, separate position watchers Sonnet every 15 mins and a weekly review again with Fable. I used Claude Code routines with rules/journals in GitHub, and Finance District's Agent Wallet for checking balances, trades and getting paid data. 

Feel free to DM and I'll share with you the exact prompt :)
